in_text_mentions: A 59-year-old male presented to the emergency department with left upper arm pain, which began abruptly while lifting some plywood about six days prior. On examination, he had significant tenderness at the proximal biceps and significant pain with passive range of motion as well as three out of five strength. There was also a large, soft tissue defect at his proximal bicep with ecchymosis. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) revealed a proximal rupture of the long head of the biceps tendon (LHBT) (Images 1–3).

in_text_mentions: On presentation, he had a positive hook test, and the distal biceps tendon could not be palpated in his antecubital fossa. His neurovascular status was intact. MRI showed the complete rupture of the distal biceps tendon insertion associated with an 8.5 cm proximal retraction and mild tendinosis with partial tearing at the common extensor tendon origin (Figure 1). The patient was informed regarding his options of conservative and surgical repair versus reconstruction and the patient elected surgical repair of the distal biceps tendon. Surgery was performed two months after the initial injury.

After three months, he presented with increased muscle bulk and ongoing weakness, prompting an evaluation at our center. Upon clinical examination, we observed a positive reverse Popeye sign (Figure 1A, 1B), a negative biceps squeeze, and a hook test indicative of complete distal biceps tendon rupture, resulting in grade 4 weakness in supination and flexion.
